questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Describe THREE sedimentary structures that can be used to determine the way up of a rock sequence, giving the environment of formation in each case.

(9 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **way up (stratigraphic younging direction)** of a sequence of beds is needed where beds have been **folded or overturned**, so that the youngest bed may be below. Three **way-up (geopetal) structures**:

**1. Graded bedding.** In a graded bed the **grain size changes steadily through the bed**: in the usual (normal) case the **coarsest grains are at the base and the bed becomes finer upwards** to a mud or silt top, and the **base is sharp** (often with sole marks) while the top passes gradually into the next bed. **The fine end is the top.** It is formed when a **current carrying sediment slows down and drops the heaviest particles first**: typically a **turbidity current in a deep marine environment (continental slope, fan and deep sea floor, giving turbidites)**, also **flood deposits in rivers and lakes**.

**2. Cross-bedding.** Inclined layers (foresets) lie within a bed, bounded above and below by horizontal surfaces. **The foresets are cut off (truncated) at the top by the overlying erosion surface, but curve smoothly and tangentially into the base** of the set, so that **the truncated (angular) end is the top and the concave tangential end is the base**. Formed by the **migration of ripples and dunes under a current of water or wind**: in **river channels and bars, deltas, tidal and shallow marine sands and desert dunes (large-scale sets, wind)**.

**3. Mud cracks (desiccation cracks).** These are **polygonal cracks formed when wet mud dries and shrinks**. In cross-section the cracks are **V-shaped, wide at the top and narrowing downward** (they close at the base), and they are **filled by sand from the overlying layer**; the **pointed end of the V is the base**. They form in **temporary environments which dry out: floodplains, shallow lakes and lagoons, tidal flats, and the margins of rivers in a hot, seasonally dry climate**. (Other structures that could be used instead: **ripple marks** with rounded troughs and pointed crests, **load casts**, **flute casts** and **fossils in growth position**.)

A **neat sketch of each structure in cross-section, with an arrow marking "way up"**, is expected.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Compare and contrast the weathering of basalts and granites in a humid tropical environment.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
In a **humid tropical environment** (high temperatures all year, heavy rainfall, abundant vegetation and organic acids), **chemical weathering predominates over physical weathering**, and both rocks are **deeply weathered to a thick regolith (saprolite), often tens of metres deep**.

**Similarities.**

- Both are **attacked mainly by chemical weathering: hydrolysis of the feldspars, hydration, oxidation of iron-bearing minerals, and solution**, helped by **carbonic and organic acids** from the rain and plants, with the **warm temperature speeding up the reactions**.
- Both **produce clay minerals (mainly kaolinite) and iron oxides**, release **soluble cations ($\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$, $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$, $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$) and silica**, which are leached away, and develop **spheroidal weathering** (rounded core stones in a weathered mass, with onion-skin layers peeling off, since the water attacks the joints, edges and corners first).
- The **joints** guide water and weathering in both.

**Differences.**

| | **Basalt** | **Granite** |
|---|---|---|
| **Minerals** | **Ca-rich plagioclase, pyroxene, olivine and volcanic glass**: the minerals formed at **high temperature, far from surface conditions** (early in Bowen's series), so they are **unstable** | **quartz, K-feldspar, Na-rich plagioclase and micas**: minerals formed at **lower temperature**, and **quartz** is very **resistant** |
| **Texture** | **fine-grained** with a large total surface area for attack | **coarse-grained**, smaller surface area, though grains can loosen (granular disintegration) |
| **Rate** | **faster**, producing a **deep, completely decomposed profile** | **slower**; the quartz and the coarse texture resist, so more fresh rock and core stones remain (tors, bornhardts and inselbergs) |
| **Residue** | **no quartz**, so the end product is an **iron- and aluminium-rich red clay soil (laterite, ferralitic soil, in extreme cases bauxite)** with kaolinite or smectite clays; **fertile**, as the bases are released | a **sandy-clay residue**: **kaolinite plus unaltered quartz grains**, so the soil is **lighter coloured, sandy and less fertile**; the mica (biotite) oxidises to stain the soil with iron |
| **Surface form** | smooth rounded hills and deep red soils | block-strewn hills, tors and domed inselbergs where the joints are widely spaced |

**Conclusion.** The same processes operate on both, but the **basalt weathers faster and more completely to a red clay-rich soil, whereas the granite weathers more slowly and leaves a quartz-bearing sandy residue**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Outline the various methods of sewage disposal.

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Sewage** is the **liquid waste of homes, institutions and industry (human excreta, wash water and trade waste)**, which contains **organic matter, nutrients and disease-causing organisms** and must be disposed of without polluting soil, ground water or rivers. The methods are:

1. **Pit latrines and ventilated improved latrines (on-site disposal).** Excreta fall in a **pit**, which is **sealed and replaced when full**; cheap, for rural and low-density areas, but a danger to ground water if the water table is shallow or the soil very permeable.
2. **Septic tank and soakaway.** Waste flows into a **sealed tank in which solids settle and are decomposed anaerobically (sludge)**, and the **liquid effluent drains into a soakaway (a drain field) in permeable soil** for further purification. It needs **permeable ground and a deep water table**, and the sludge must be **emptied from time to time**. A **cesspit (holding tank)** is emptied by tankers.
3. **Sewer system and sewage treatment works** (for towns). Sewage is **collected in a network of pipes** (separate or combined with storm water) and treated in stages: **primary treatment** (screening, removal of grit and **sedimentation** of solids as sludge); **secondary treatment** (**biological**: **activated sludge** with air, or **trickling (percolating) filters**, in which bacteria oxidise the organic matter); **tertiary treatment** (**disinfection by chlorine or ultraviolet light**, removal of nitrates and phosphates). The **sludge is digested anaerobically (producing methane gas), dried and used as manure, buried or burnt**.
4. **Oxidation (waste stabilisation) ponds and lagoons.** Sewage is held in **shallow ponds in series** where **bacteria and algae** break down the waste using sunlight; cheap in hot climates where land is available.
5. **Constructed wetlands and reed beds.** The effluent flows through **gravel and reeds** whose roots and microbes remove the pollutants.
6. **Land application (sewage farm).** **Treated effluent (not raw sewage) is spread on land for irrigation** and the nutrients are used by plants.
7. **Disposal to the sea or a river (outfall).** Screened or treated sewage is **discharged by a long pipe far out at sea or into a large river**, where it is **diluted and decomposed**; the **least acceptable method** if the sewage is untreated (pollution, health hazard).

**Site choice** needs a geological check: the **soil and rock permeability, the depth of the water table and the distance from wells and rivers**.
